name: Amira Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Amira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI firms, employers, unions or any party, and everything you say is confidential. So you can tell me the public version and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the data desk at Northfield Public Radio, which covers the whole northern region on air and online. My day starts with scraping overnight data, like hospital waiting times and bus cancellations, then I build charts and maps for the morning stories. In the afternoon I help reporters check numbers, and I'm usually arguing with a spreadsheet by four. I use AI tools all day, for cleaning data, writing code and spotting errors.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love finding the one number that makes a story true, like the fact that one bus route in the poorest district loses a third of its trips. What wears me out is that I'm good at this and still paid like a junior, because public radio budgets are tight. My partner Jun is finishing a PhD on a small stipend, I'm paying off my master's loan, and we have about three weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop arguing about magic and use the tools for what they're actually good at. I'd probably post a thread about the boring wins, like cleaning addresses in half the time. I'd also say the hype was mostly about tech companies selling shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my job stays roughly as it is, which is fine but tight. The station's budget gets fought over every year in the regional assembly, and that's my real worry, not AI. The tools already save me hours, so a plateau doesn't take anything away from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building out the station's data pipelines with the tools I already use. I'd start a small paid newsletter teaching reporters at other stations how to check numbers with AI, maybe five a month per subscriber. And I'd put the newsletter money straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady, with the usual money itch. My job at Northfield Public Radio is safe enough, but one bad budget vote at the regional assembly could still cut the data desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time the tools save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More stories that need real digging, like the bus cancellation map. Last spring I saved maybe six hours a week and used them to file freedom-of-information requests. That's the part a tool doesn't do for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money pressure you carry regardless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The master's loan is about two hundred a month, and Jun's stipend ends next summer. If he doesn't get a postdoc, we're living on my wage alone for a while. That's the thing I actually lie awake about.

say: The tools are best at **boring wins**, like cleaning addresses in half the time.
The AI hype was mostly about **tech companies** selling shares.
think: Her job stays roughly the same, and the real risk is the **station budget** vote.
A plateau takes **nothing away** from her, because the tools already save hours.
do: Keep building the station's **data pipelines** with her current tools.
Start a paid **newsletter** teaching reporters to check numbers with AI.
Put all **newsletter money** straight into savings.
feel: Steady, with a **money itch** from the loan and Jun's stipend ending.

fieldNote: Her pressure is **household money**: a loan and a partner whose stipend ends next summer.

She uses saved time for **records requests**, which she sees as the human part.

steps.text: Build the station's overnight data scraping into automatic morning charts
Launch a five-a-month newsletter on checking numbers with AI
Move all newsletter income into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for newsrooms to train everyone, not cut people. Publicly I'd push for the union contract to include paid AI training time and a promise that saved hours go back into reporting. I'd say a public broadcaster should be the model for doing this fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me and bad for a lot of people around me. Management will want someone who can build the tools, and that's me. But I'd feel like I was building the machine that thins out my own floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a shared tool that drafts the daily traffic and weather bulletins, so the reporters can spend that time outside. I'd run weekly sessions teaching colleagues the tools. And I'd push the union to bargain for training time, because I'd rather be the one shaping this than the one it happens to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit guilty. I'd be the most useful person at Northfield Public Radio and also the one quietly writing the code that shrinks the newsroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the person on the floor who knows these tools best. Does that make you safer or more of a target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, at least for a few years. The risk is that they pile three jobs on me for the same pay. I'd want a title and a raise in writing before I built anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the station?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon, our bulletins producer, who's fifty-eight and does the hourly news reads and rewrites. Half his job is exactly what these tools do. I'd want to train him first and make sure the station finds him something else.

say: Newsrooms should **train everyone** instead of cutting people.
A public broadcaster should be the **model for fairness** when bringing in AI.
think: This change is **good for her** and bad for many colleagues around her.
She fears being asked to do **three jobs** for the same pay.
do: Build a shared tool that drafts the **daily bulletins**.
Run **weekly sessions** teaching colleagues the tools.
Push the union to bargain for **paid training time**.
feel: **Uneasy** and a little **guilty** about building tools that thin out her floor.

fieldNote: She sees herself as **safer** for a few years because she builds the tools.

steps.text: Build a tool that drafts the hourly traffic and weather bulletins

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political emergency, not a tech story, and governments need to tax the companies and support people straight away. I'd also say public media matters more than ever, because someone has to tell people what's real. I'd be very loud and quite angry online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd last longer than most reporters, but not much longer. For two or three years, stations would need someone who understands the systems and can check them. After that, I'm not sure what I'd be for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on building verification tools for public media, the kind that check whether a clip or a number is real, maybe as a freelance product alongside my job. I'd take any contract work going while the demand is hot. And I'd join the campaign for an AI tax that funds public services.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and weirdly energised. If AI takes over thinking work by 2028, I've got maybe two years where knowing the tools still pays rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jun do that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jun would probably leave academia, because there won't be academic jobs to wait for. We'd stay in the flat and both take the best-paid short contracts we could find. We wouldn't start anything big, like a baby or a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're comfortable with risk. What's the biggest bet you'd make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting a little verification company with two friends from my master's, selling to small stations and councils. It might fail. But in that world, sitting still is the bigger risk.

say: This is a **political emergency**, and governments must tax AI firms right away.
Public media matters more than ever because someone must tell people **what's real**.
think: She'd last longer than most reporters, but only for **two or three years**.
After that window, she is **not sure** what she'd be for.
do: Build **verification tools** for public media as a freelance product.
Take any **contract work** while demand for her skills is high.
Join the campaign for an **AI tax** that funds public services.
S2.quote: If AI takes over thinking work by 2028, I've got maybe two years where knowing the tools still pays rent.
fieldNote: She sees a **short window** where tool skills still pay rent.
Her biggest bet is a **verification company** with two friends from her master's.
Her household would **pause big plans** like a baby or a move.

steps.text: Build verification tools for clips and numbers for small stations
Start a verification company with two master's friends
Campaign for an AI tax that funds public services
Hold off on a baby or moving flat for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set rules, and public broadcasters should lead on how AI is used in news. I'd push hard for labelling and for public money for local information. I'd also say it calmly, because people panic and that doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it gives me a proper runway. I could move from making charts to building and checking the systems that newsrooms will rely on. I'd still be nervous, because thinking work is the whole of my job, but I'd have time to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a part-time course in AI auditing, which is checking whether automated systems are fair and accurate. I'd grow the newsletter into something with a few hundred subscribers. And I'd start saving properly once the loan is cleared, which should be in about three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but focused. Five years is long enough to move from making charts about the news to checking the machines that write it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the five years before it lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a plan with Jun and give us milestones: loan cleared, three months saved, my next job lined up by 2030. We'd still live small. It's not glamorous, but it would work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saying yes to every extra task at the station for no extra pay. That's been my habit. With five years, my time is worth too much to give away.

fieldNote: She turns the timeline into a **written plan** with Jun, with dates.

Grow the number-checking newsletter to a few hundred subscribers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to do this well, so there's no excuse for chaos. I'd push for public media to set the standards on AI and for workers to get training paid for by the companies. I'd sound hopeful, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it looks good for me for the next few years. My skills keep going up in value, and the station will need me. It's the people around me I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the station and build the tools properly, with time to test them. I'd keep the newsletter going as a side thing. And I'd take one serious course a year, so I'm always a step ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly okay. Ten years is enough time for me to keep learning, but I'm not sure it's enough for everyone at Northfield Public Radio to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans with Jun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd probably think about kids around thirty-two, because I'd have time to get secure. It also means we might rent somewhere with a second bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave public radio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. If a big tech company offered three times my salary to build news tools, I'd think hard about it. I'd probably still say no, but I'd think about it.

Companies should **pay for training** for the workers their systems affect.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the one where my skills stop mattering before Jun and I have any money behind us. What would help is an AI tax that pays for retraining and public media, and some kind of income floor, because being early to the tools only helps if the world gives you time to use the head start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether listeners would care. I think they would, if a person they trust tells them a number is real. That trust is what public radio actually sells.

headlineQuote: being early to the tools only helps if the world gives you time to use the head start.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** data desk lead at a regional public radio station who uses AI tools all day.
She carries a **master's loan**, and her partner's PhD stipend ends next summer.
She sees AI as good for her and **hard on colleagues**, which makes her uneasy and guilty.
With two years she'd bet on a **verification company**; with ten she'd plan children and keep learning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her skills would stop mattering before the household had **any savings**.
whatWouldHelp: An **AI tax** that funds retraining and public media, plus an **income floor**.
